title: Bullet Trains' 15m Nose Isn't for Wind Drag?｜So That's Why
description:
Why do Japanese Shinkansen bullet trains have 15-meter needle noses, while Taiwan High Speed Rail runs just as fast at 300 km/h with a shorter nose?
For anyone whose ears have popped in a rail tunnel or wondered why bullet train noses look like needles or duckbills.
From the 1964 Tokaido Shinkansen and 1975 Sanyo tunnel booms to micro-pressure waves, kingfishers, and Taiwan's wider tunnels, here is the three-way balance between speed, tunnel width, and passenger seats (Note: JR Central and THSR do not publish separate nose lengths for N700S and N700ST; 500 Series retirement per JR West 2026-06-22 notice).

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.
Data as of 2026-11-18.

thumbnail.headline: Why **Shorter**?
thumbnail.sub: Before it exits, the tunnel booms!

chapters.chief-era-handoff-bridge: Next-Gen Trains Arrive in Kaohsiung: Two Details to Spot

p001.text: Chief! Japan's nose is 15m—why is fast Taiwan HSR's shorter?

p002.text: That's the key! If long noses only cut open-air wind drag, equal speed would need equal length—everyone guessed wrong!

p003.text: The real enemy isn't flatland—it's the split second a train hits a tunnel.

p004.text: Early bullet trains ran with blunt round noses, yet a Japanese test train later stretched to about 22 meters;

p005.text: To tame invisible tunnel shockwaves, engineers fired nose models down pipes and looked to diving waterbirds!

p006.text: Today let's explore how tunnels stretched bullet train noses—and how Taiwan High Speed Rail shortened them back!

p007.text: In 1964, Japan's first Tokaido Shinkansen opened with a plump round dumpling nose.

p008.text: With no long nose at all, it ran smoothly and fast across open plains.

p009.text: Wait—at those speeds, wouldn't a sharp, stretched nose slice through the air like a knife and save power?

p010.text: A pointed nose cuts a bit of drag, but Japan's Railway Technical Research Institute measured whole long trains.

p011.text: When over a dozen cars charge ahead together, air rubs and builds skin friction all along the outer walls;

p012.text: Most air drag isn't at the nose at all—it comes from the long side walls and turbulent gaps between cars!

p013.text: So on open plains, a smooth rounded nose is plenty; there's zero need for a 15-meter snout.

p014.text: Yet in March 1975, right before the westward Sanyo Shinkansen opened to Hakata, something bizarre struck!

p015.text: A round-nosed test train plunged into a long mountain tunnel, still kilometers away from the far exit;

p016.text: And yet, kilometers ahead, the far tunnel portal suddenly erupted with a cannon-like BOOM!

p017.text: The train was still kilometers inside—why did the exit boom like a fighter jet? Did it go supersonic?

p019.text: Even at 300 km/h, a bullet train is only a quarter of Mach 1—what raced ahead was an invisible pressure wave!

p020.text: Outdoors, air escapes in every direction, but a sealed tunnel acts like a giant bicycle pump;

p021.text: The train nose slams in like a plunger, squeezing out a compression wave that races ahead at the speed of sound!

p022.text: Outrunning the train, it bursts out the exit as a 'tunnel boom' or micro-pressure wave—and sound wasn't the worst part!

p023.text: Beyond audible blasts above 20 hertz, it also carries infrasound below 20 hertz—

p024.text: Your ears can't hear it, yet it rattles sliding doors and windows in nearby homes, terrifying residents!

p025.text: Wait—the 1964 train used tunnels daily! Why did Sanyo boom?

p026.text: Satoru Ozawa found why: old Tokaido tracks used gravel ballast that cushioned waves.

p027.text: New Sanyo tunnels used smooth, low-maintenance concrete slabs; without gravel gaps to damp the wave in long tunnels,

p028.text: The rear of the wave traveled faster through air warmed by the front, steepening into a cliff that boomed at the exit!

p029.text: They couldn't move mountains or rip up all that concrete—so how did engineers silence the tunnel exit?

p030.text: Since they couldn't flatten the wave mid-tunnel, they tackled the source: the nose entering at second zero!

p031.text: It still squeezes into the same narrow tunnel—how can nose shape alone quiet an exit kilometers away?

p032.text: What matters isn't total air pushed, but how steeply tunnel pressure spikes the instant the nose enters!

p033.text: A blunt nose slams pressure up like a cliff; a longer nose pushes air gradually, turning that cliff into a gentle ramp!

p034.text: Then wouldn't sharpening the nose into a straight, pencil-point cone solve everything?

p035.text: Not so fast! RTRI tested blunt, sharp-cone, and gradually widening bullet noses—and the sharp cone still boomed!

p036.text: A straight cone widens evenly, so doubling width quadruples area—pushing a sudden surge of air near the back!

p037.text: Only a 'paraboloid of revolution' adds equal cross-sectional area per meter, keeping micro-pressure waves minimal!

p038.text: Engineers also slimmed and rounded the car body so air slips past the sides instead of being shoved forward.

p039.text: And they built vented 'tunnel hoods' at portals to bleed pressure—remember those hoods for Taiwan's story soon!

p040.text: With paraboloid noses plus portal hoods working together, surely the problem was solved for good?

p041.text: Then came a catch! In the '90s JR West aimed for 300 km/h—and power laws hit.

p042.text: Open-air drag grows with speed squared, micro-pressure waves with speed cubed or more, and wind noise to the sixth power!

p043.text: Push speed up just 10 percent, and that tunnel-exit boom roughly jumps by over 30 percent!

p044.text: Worse still was Sanyo terrain! Test engineer Eiji Nakatsu recalled that 51 percent of the route is tunnels.

p045.text: Japanese Shinkansen tunnels are only about 65 square meters wide—stuffing a 3.4-meter train in is like threading a needle!

p046.text: During high-speed trials, booms and low-frequency vibrations angered residents 400 meters from tunnel portals;

p047.text: Backed into a corner, the team had to abandon test runs above 350 kilometers per hour!

p048.text: Even tests halted! With physics that harsh, who on earth could save them?

p049.text: The savior had wings! In a meeting, a young colleague remarked that entering a tunnel felt like the car shrank.

p050.text: That sparked birdwatcher Nakatsu—doesn't nature have an animal diving daily into high resistance?

p051.text: He thought of the kingfisher, plunging fast from low-drag air into dense water with almost zero splash!

p052.text: Wait—did engineers just trace a bird's beak with a ruler to build the new train nose?

p053.text: No way! How would a flat beak fit a cab? Remember the pipe-shot test—they fired nose models into pipes to measure pressure;

p054.text: Then aerospace supercomputers ran simulations to find the ideal paraboloid with the gentlest pressure rise.

p055.text: When they compared that computed cross-section curve, it matched a kingfisher's beak-to-head profile almost exactly!

p056.text: Biomechanics researchers later tested 71 kingfisher beak shapes, confirming that smooth transition cuts entry drag.

p057.text: And there's more! They also borrowed owl feather serrations to quiet wind roar from roof pantographs.

p058.text: In March 1997, the 15m-nosed 500 Series debuted at 300 km/h in Japan!

p059.text: Shin-Osaka to Hakata dropped by 15 minutes, and Nakatsu's paper recorded over 10% lower power use than the 300 Series.

p060.text: Fast and thrifty! So every Shinkansen nose after that must have grown longer and longer, right?

p061.text: Quite the opposite! The next 700 Series cut the nose back to 9.2m!

p062.text: What?! After calculating that ultimate 15-meter nose, why chop nearly 6 meters off the next train?

p063.text: Japanese car engineers noted the catch: lead-car length is fixed—if the nose takes half, where do riders sit?

p064.text: The cylindrical long nose lost seats and misaligned doors with the 300 Series, creating platform headaches!

p065.text: To win back seats, multi-paraboloids formed a duckbill—quiet at 285 km/h.

p066.text: Next, the N700S kept its lead car at 27.35m—not a millimeter longer;

p067.text: Instead, 'Dual Supreme Wing' ridges sculpt airflow along both sides, cutting tunnel booms and tail-car sway!

p068.text: Yet faster runs in narrow bores need long noses—like Tohoku's E5;

p069.text: And the 360 km/h ALFA-X test train tried ~16m and 22m noses!

p070.text: Why is Taiwan's shorter? Based on the 700, the 700T runs 300 km/h with an 8m nose!

p071.text: Faster yet 1.2m shorter—why don't Taiwan's tunnels boom?

p072.text: Tunnel width! Taiwan HSR bores top 90 sq m—nearly half bigger than Japan's!

p073.text: In a wider bore, air has ample room to slip past both sides as the train enters, weakening the compression wave.

p074.text: JSME records show Taiwan also built 30–40m slanted vented portal hoods!

p075.text: Wide tunnels plus vented hoods relieve pressure twice—so trains stay quiet without giant noses, saving room for your seats!

p076.text: Aha! Instead of long noses cutting seats every trip, wide tunnels solved it upfront!

p077.text: By 2026, this nose-vs-tunnel duel hit a generational handoff!

p078.text: Under JR West's current plan, the iconic 500 Series ends regular scheduled runs on January 13, 2027;

p079.text: In July 2027 it retires, ending a 30-year high-speed career.

p080.text: Taiwan's first Dual-Wing N700ST reached Kaohsiung Port in Aug 2026;

p081.text: Passenger service starts in late 2027—next time you're on the platform, know which two details to spot first?

p082.text: Check the nose lines—duckbill or new dual-wing ridges—then look down the track for that slanted concrete tunnel hood!

p083.text: Every meter of nose length is a precise engineering balance among speed, tunnel bore, and passenger seats.

p084.text: Tell us in the comments: when your bullet train enters a tunnel, do your ears pop or barely feel a thing?

p085.text: If you love unpacking everyday transport secrets, subscribe to So That's Why—see you next time!
